title: ～ように見える — “looks like ～ / seems ～”
summary: Describes how something appears to the eye, either as a comparison (looks like a sheep) or as an impression (looks tired). It attaches to a plain-form verb or adjective (な-adj + な), or noun + の. It is based on appearance, not on hearsay.

body.p: The speaker describes what it looks like, without saying it is true. 疲れているように見える means “appears tired.” The real condition may be different.
With a noun, the thing looks similar to something else: 羊のように見える雲. In a photo, 実物より大きいように見える shows that the impression differs from the real size.

body.h: Difference from ～そうだ and ～みたい
body.p: ～そうに見える is also visual. ～ように見える can be used with a wider range, including when comparing. ～ように見える is natural for polite writing; ～みたいに見える is casual.

examples.ja: その雲（くも）は羊（ひつじ）のように見（み）える。
examples.romaji: Sono kumo wa hitsuji no you ni mieru.
examples.tr: That cloud looks like a sheep.

examples.ja: この写真（しゃしん）だと、実物（じつぶつ）より大（おお）きいように見（み）える。
examples.romaji: Kono shashin da to, jitsubutsu yori ookii you ni mieru.
examples.tr: In this photo, it looks bigger than it really is.

examples.ja: 少（すこ）し疲（つか）れているように見（み）えるけど、大丈夫（だいじょうぶ）ですか。
examples.romaji: Sukoshi tsukarete iru you ni mieru kedo, daijoubu desu ka.
examples.tr: You look a little tired; are you all right?

pitfalls: It describes sight only. For what you heard, use ～そうだ (hearsay) or ～らしい.
A noun needs の (羊のように), not な.
